source.citation: Shende T, Andaluri G, Suri RP. Power density modulated ultrasonic degradation of perfluoroalkyl substances with and without sparging Argon. Ultrasonics Sonochemistry. 2021;76:105639.

evidence_passages.passage: We evaluated the ultrasonic degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) at various power densities (30 W/L–262 W/L) with and without sparging Argon. We observed pseudo-first-order degradation kinetics at an initial PFASs concentration of 100 nM over a range of power density.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Page 1, Section 2.2 Sonication experiment and PFAS analysis
evidence_passages.passage: The mixture of PFOS and PFOA was sonicated at various power densities by varying volume (50–500 mL) of the aqueous solution with and without sparging Argon… The sonication experiments were conducted at constant ultrasonic power of 120 W in duplicate.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Page 1, Section 2.2 Sonication experiment and PFAS analysis
evidence_passages.passage: It should be noted that fluoride formation (i.e. defluorination) was not measured in this study as the initial concentration of PFOA and PFOS in the aqueous solution was low. However, short-chain PFASs (C3–C7) were monitored.

evidence_passages.page_or_section: Page 1, Section 2.2 Sonication experiment and PFAS analysis
evidence_passages.passage: Detailed information of the experimental procedure, setup and by-products formations during sonolytic degradation of PFOA and PFOS were reported elsewhere [25,26].

source_limitations: Study evaluates parent PFAS removal kinetics but does not quantify fluoride or total defluorination, limiting conclusions about mineralization.
Short-chain PFAS transformation products are monitored, but fluorine mass balance is not closed.
Initial PFAS concentrations (100 nM) are low, constraining analytical options for inorganic fluoride measurement and possibly affecting detection limits for products.
Argon sparging and laboratory reactor geometry may not directly translate to full-scale systems.

sources.citation: Ren Z, Bergmann U, Leiviskä T. Reductive degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid in complex water matrices by using the UV/sulfite process. Water Research. 2021;205:117676.

evidence_chunks.text: The results showed that the concentration of PFOA was below the detection limit (10 μg/L) after 1 h (conditions: C0 10 mg/L, initial pH = 10, sulfite 10 mM) while 89% defluorination was achieved after 24 h. Using a higher initial pH (pH = 12) greatly enhanced the PFOA degradation as 100% degradation and 98% defluorination were achieved after 24 h.

evidence_chunks.section: Page 2, Section 2.2 Reductive degradation of PFOA
evidence_chunks.text: Unless otherwise specified, the dosage of sulfite was 10 mM and the initial concentration of PFOA was 10 mg/L (24.15 μM). Four initial pH values (9, 10, 11 and 12) were chosen to investigate the effect of pH.

During the process, short-chain perfluorinated carboxylic acids (PFCAs, C < 7) and hydrogen substituted compounds were detected, which implies that chain-shortening and H/F change reactions had occurred. Moreover, this confirmed the generation of sulfonated and unsaturated intermediates during the process, which disclosed valuable new mechanistic insights into PFOA degradation.

Hydrated electrons (eaq−, E = −2.9 V) generated by advanced reduction processes (ARPs) have been proved to be a promising approach to eliminate various per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in water. In this study, the decomposition of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in a complex water matrix by eaq− generated from the UV/sulfite process was investigated.

The presence of carbonate (> 5 mM), nitrate (> 2 mM) and humic acid (> 25 mg/L) showed a significant negative effect on PFOA degradation via a UV blocking effect or quenching of hydrated electrons while the presence of chloride and phosphate had a smaller effect on PFOA degradation.

The concentration of PFAS reported in contaminated water has been usually at the ng/L to μg/L level … Therefore, some pretreatment methods like membrane technologies and sorption/desorption are preferred to concentrate PFASs before applying the UV/sulfite process.

source_limitations: Single-target study focused on PFOA; does not include other PFAS classes.
Defluorination is tracked via fluoride ISE; total fluorine or organofluorine mass balance is not closed.
Matrix complexity is represented by added inorganic anions and humic acid rather than real field samples.
Detection limit for PFOA (10 μg/L) may not be representative of state-of-the-art analytical sensitivity.
sources.title: Reductive degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid in complex water matrices by using the UV/sulfite process

sources.citation: O’Connor N. Forever No More: Complete mineralization of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) using an optimized UV/sulfite/iodide system. In: Aqueous Electron Initiated Destruction of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS). PhD thesis, Royal Military College of Canada; 2024. Chapter 3. Related journal article: Sci Total Environ. 2023;888:164137.

evidence_chunks.text: This study investigates the use of sulfite and iodide in a bicarbonate-buffered alkaline system activated with ultraviolet (UV) light to destroy PFAS. The UV/sulfite/iodide system creates a reductive environment through the generation of aqueous electrons, which can degrade PFAS.

The extent of degradation and defluorination was explored for perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), 6:2 fluorotelomer sulfonic acid (6:2 FTS), and perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS). An initial UV/sulfite/iodide system achieved 100% degradation and >90% defluorination for PFOS, PFOA, and 6:2 FTS, but was not capable of completely degrading PFBS.

Novel identification of −F/+H perfluoropropane sulfonic acid (PFPS) and −F/+H perfluoroethane sulfonic acid (PFES) following degradation of PFOS confirms C–C bond cleavage, and different isomers of −F/+H PFOS confirms the potential for C–F bond cleavage to occur throughout the perfluoroalkyl chain.

The optimal protocol found in this study involved an elevated initial sulfite concentration and adding additional sulfite at regular intervals during UV-activation, achieving >99.9% destruction and complete quantitative defluorination of PFBS.

It is the overall recommendation of this thesis that this work be further pursued for scale-up and commercialization so it can be added to the growing list of effective PFAS treatment options. Without additional optimization, this technology would excel for the flow-through destruction of high concentrations of PFCAs in simple and moderately complex aqueous matrices.
Destruction is measured as both a loss of the initial PFAS and a quantitative recovery of the resultant fluoride ions.

source_limitations: Thesis format; overlapping content with a peer-reviewed article but thesis itself is not peer-reviewed.
Emphasis on relatively high PFAS concentrations compared with typical environmental waters.
Fluoride recovery is emphasized, but full fluorine mass balance including volatile organofluorine is not comprehensively closed.
Matrix complexity is evaluated mainly with bicarbonate buffer and added scavengers rather than real wastewaters.
sources.title: Forever No More: Complete mineralization of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) using an optimized UV/sulfite/iodide system (thesis chapter)

sources.citation: Pinkard B, Smith SM, Vorarath P, et al. Degradation and Defluorination of Ultra Short‑, Short‑, and Long-Chain PFASs in High Total Dissolved Solids Solutions by Hydrothermal Alkaline Treatment—Closing the Fluorine Mass Balance. ACS ES&T Engineering. 2024;4:2810–2818.

evidence_chunks.text: In this effort, a mixture of ultra short-, short-, and long-chain PFASs in an aqueous matrix with high total dissolved solids (TDS) content is processed using hydrothermal alkaline treatment (HALT). Degradation and defluorination are assessed at various HALT operating conditions (T = 250−350 °C, NaOH = 2−16 wt %).

In all experiments, the fluorine mass balance is near-stoichiometric at optimized conditions, and a “multiple-lines-of-evidence” analytical approach including targeted LC−MS/MS analysis, free fluoride quantification, and total organic fluorine measurements strongly suggests that there is minimal undesired organofluorine byproduct formation.
Overall, this study robustly demonstrates that HALT can facilitate complete degradation and defluorination of ultra short-, short-, and long-chain PFASs in a challenging solution (≈10 wt % TDS).

A novel, multiple-lines-of-evidence approach with a suite of analytical techniques is leveraged to track the fluorine mass balance, demonstrating effective degradation and defluorination of PFASs in the HALT environment.

Six groupings of PFASs were tested in this study, including PFCAs, a perfluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acid (PFECA), polyfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (polyFCAs), PFSAs, fluoroalkane sulfonamides (FASAs), and a bis-(perfluoroalkane sulfonyl)imidic acid (PFSI)… compositions within these groupings … span across ultra short-, short-, and long chain homologues.

source_limitations: Bench-scale study using synthetic high-TDS solutions; not direct field implementation.
Focus is on aqueous phase; volatile organofluorine species are inferred to be minimal but not directly trapped in a gas-phase train.
HALT conditions (250–350 °C, high NaOH) differ substantially from many competing destruction technologies and are specific to concentrated brines.
Study is designed around a specific mixture of PFAS and does not include polymeric PFAS.
sources.title: Degradation and Defluorination of Ultra Short‑, Short‑, and Long-Chain PFASs in High Total Dissolved Solids Solutions by Hydrothermal Alkaline Treatment—Closing the Fluorine Mass Balance

sources.citation: Smith SM, Pinkard BR, Zweifel T, et al. Demonstration of hydrothermal alkaline treatment for PFAS destruction in industrial wastewater: assessment of degradation, defluorination, fluorine mass balance, and potential for volatile organofluorine formation. ChemRxiv; 2025. Preprint.

evidence_chunks.text: In this study, a commercial-scale HALT system was employed to degrade and defluorinate PFAS in a concentrated industrial wastewater stream produced from an ion exchange resin regeneration process. Numerous operating conditions were tested to assess the extent of PFAS degradation, extent of defluorination, and any production of fluorinated byproducts under relatively mild HALT conditions.

Under a range of operating conditions (T: 300–350 °C, [NaOH]: 0.1–0.5 M), HALT displayed the ability to degrade and defluorinate target FCAs with high efficacy. Near-100% degradation was achieved for FCAs across all tested operating conditions.

At the higher tested temperature, near-complete closure of the fluorine mass balance was observed, with dissolved inorganic fluoride formed as the final reaction product and no observable VOF generation. However, operating at higher throughputs, lower temperatures, and lower NaOH concentrations led to production of inert 1H-perfluoroalkane VOFs.

Overall, this study demonstrates that HALT can be successfully incorporated as part of an industrial wastewater treatment train to degrade and defluorinate PFAS in concentrated liquids with complex water chemistries and high TDS. HALT efficacy is relatively agnostic to PFAS chain length and can be tuned to target FCAs or PFSAs with various resulting practical trade-offs.
Some precipitation of hard minerals was observed (e.g., Ca, Mg), likely including CaF2 and MgF2.

source_limitations: Preprint; not yet peer-reviewed at time of inspection.
Industrial wastewater composition and PFAS profile are specific to an ion-exchange regeneration brine and may not generalize to other matrices.
Fluorine mass balance does not include direct quantitative speciation of all volatile organofluorine compounds at sub-trace levels.
Focus is on fluorinated carboxylic acids (FCAs); perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids are present only as minor constituents.
sources.title: Demonstration of hydrothermal alkaline treatment for PFAS destruction in industrial wastewater: assessment of degradation, defluorination, fluorine mass balance, and potential for volatile organofluorine formation

sources.citation: Harrison BG, Major DW, Kinsman LL, et al. Smoldering Treatment of PFAS: Investigation of Mass Balance and Volumetric Scale Up for Field Implementation. ACS Omega. 2025;10(28):30489–30500.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, PFAS Treatment section, around lines 282–283
evidence_chunks.text: Targeted PFAS analysis measured with LC–MS/MS showed >99.9% reduction in detectable PFAS, below the method quantitation limit for all tests except for B-4 and Ca-3.

In tests without CaO, PIGE soil data demonstrated a 96–99% removal in total fluorine following smoldering (0.5–3.3 mg of F/kg of soil post-treatment)… This lower removal of total fluorine compared to targeted PFAS analysis may be attributed to fluorinated compounds outside of the targeted analytical scope.

In all test cases, the quantity of HF in emissions exceeded the quantity of targeted PFAS in emissions, suggesting mineralization is achieved. Mass recoveries of HF emissions are summarized in Table S11.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, Fluorine Mass Balance section, lines 315–337
evidence_chunks.text: Comparing the results of fluorine mass on pretreatment soils with PIGE analysis of emission GAC and post-treatment sand and fluorine recovered during burnout tests, a fluorine mass balance of each test could be generated… Overall recovery of fluorine ranged from 68 to 128%.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, HF Emissions section, lines 409–409
evidence_chunks.text: The sum of the total mass emitted as HF and as organic fluorine in the post-treatment soil was <2% of the original, pretreatment fluorine mass. These results align with the Phase 1 column tests and suggest that PFAS was mineralized during treatment with a minimal release of HF in the process emissions.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, HF Emissions section, lines 410–410
evidence_chunks.text: XPS analysis indicated that CaF2 was absent in the CaO and pretreatment soils and was present in the post-treatment soils… suggests that >98% of the pretreatment PFAS mass was mineralized into CaF2 during treatment, and that potentially harmful emissions were minimized.

source_limitations: Soil-GAC systems spiked with PFOS-dominant PFAS mixture; may not represent all contaminated soil types.
Total fluorine measurements by PIGE have relatively high detection limits and cannot distinguish organic vs inorganic fluorine.
Fluorine mass balance uncertainties are large, with recoveries ranging from 68% to 128%.
Transformation products are characterized only at ultralow concentrations in emissions; many minor products remain unidentified.

sources.citation: Wood RJ, Sidnell T, Ross I, et al. Ultrasonic degradation of perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) correlated with sonochemical and sonoluminescence characterisation. Ultrasonics Sonochemistry. 2020;68:105196.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, Results and discussion, around lines 875–883
evidence_chunks.text: The results of the fluoride analysis using the fluoride probe and ALS spectrophotometry after 4 h of sonication, are shown in Table 2. Note that the theoretical yield of fluoride ions given 100% PFOS degradation is 315.9 μM (6.001 mg L−1).

Both the stoichiometric release of fluoride ions at 400, 500, and 1000 kHz and the complete degradation (at 400 and 500 kHz) indicate that sonolysis under these conditions completely degraded PFOS without significant formation of less fluorinated shorter chain PFAAs.
Trace concentrations of some shorter chain PFAAs were detected at all frequencies, but the total amount of all short chain species represented less than 1% of the total yield by mass.

Fluoride measurements via electrode analysis and those given by ALS have similar values. Within the first 2 h, both analyses show that 400 kHz has the least agreement with zero order kinetics and 1000 kHz has the best agreement.

The degradation of PFOS in solution after 4 h, analysed by ALS, is shown in Table 2… sonication at 44 kHz is ineffective… all frequencies showed an increase of ~20 °C in bulk temperature during sonication.

source_limitations: Single-compound study focusing on PFOS; results may not extend to mixed PFAS or AFFF matrices.
Fluorine mass balance is evaluated primarily via inorganic fluoride and targeted short-chain PFAAs; volatile organofluorine species are not comprehensively quantified.
Experiments conducted in relatively simple aqueous solutions, not complex natural waters or waste streams.
Detection limits and quantitation limits for transformation products are not always explicitly tied to mass-balance closure.

sources.citation: Li J, Austin C, Moore S, Pinkard BR, Novosselov IV. PFOS destruction in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chemical Engineering Journal. 2023;451(4):139063.

evidence_chunks.text: This study presents the degradation behavior of PFOS, PFHpS, and PFOA in a continuous flow SCWO reactor operated over a range of temperatures (T = 410–650 °C)… 99.999% destruction of all PFAS and complete defluorination was observed at an operating temperature of 650 °C and residence time of ∼30 s, with PFOS being the most recalcitrant.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, Section 3.4 Total PFAS Destruction/Defluorination, lines 776–799
evidence_chunks.text: Fig. 4 presents total measured PFAS and fluoride concentrations as a function of operating temperatures, as well as the overall measured fluorine mass balance at various temperatures. The total concentration of PFAS species (SumPFCAs+PFOS+PFHpS) is steadily reduced with increasing reaction temperature while the fluoride concentration increases.

SCWO operation at T > 650 °C yielded 99.9999% mineralization of PFAS… The F balance shows that >100% is ‘recovered’ based on the initial concentration at T > 580 °C, while at lower temperatures, there is an apparent deficit in the F-balance.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, Section 3.3 Gas emission, lines 721–741
evidence_chunks.text: Gas products were collected during the PFOA and PFOS experiments and semi-qualitatively analyzed by GC/MS… At lower temperatures, the analysis showed other ion fragments associated with volatile organofluorines (VOFs)… When the reaction temperature was 580 °C, no gaseous fluorine compounds were detected, and only N2, O2, CO2, and H2O were present in the gas products.

evidence_chunks.section: Main text, discussion section around lines 1145–1152
evidence_chunks.text: The VOFs were found to be more persistent than PFCA in the effluent. Though the operational temperature is driving PFAS degradation in the SCWO environment, the stability of the VOFs may dictate the minimum residence to achieve high defluorination efficiencies.

source_limitations: Access limited to an online manuscript version; some tabular and figure details may not be fully visible in the inspected text.
Fluorine mass balance does not include quantitative speciation of all volatile organofluorine species; gas-phase analysis is semi-qualitative.
Experiments use relatively high PFAS concentrations and ethanol as a co-fuel, which may not match all waste streams.
Residence time and temperature window optimized for PFOS/PFOA may not directly translate to other PFAS.

The robustness of the system has been evaluated in the presence of several different reactive radical scavengers, providing both underlying mechanistic insights, as well as allowing for the prediction of system effectiveness based on different water parameters.
It is hypothesized that the addition of an oxidative pre-treatment would further expand the effectiveness of the system to the treatment of fluorotelomer-dominant, complex aqueous matrices.

source_limitations: Chapter 4 itself is not fully excerpted in the inspected locations; detailed analytical results for complex matrices and AFFF concentrates are not directly quoted here.
Thesis is not peer-reviewed and may contain overlapping content with related journal articles.
Evidence for mineralization in complex matrices relies on the same suite of measurements as in simpler systems (parent PFAS, fluoride), with limited direct gas-phase organofluorine characterization.
